title: The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – September 25, 2026
summary: I hope you like creepy Annapurna games about protagonists with fuzzy memories exploring a weird place because we have two of them. Or you can play some soccer. - Game Informer

I hope you're getting ready to have a good weekend or whatever, but did you see that we announced the next Game Informer cover? It's Grand Theft Auto VI, baby . We have a 14-page story with exclusive interviews with members of the Rockstar development team, brand new screenshots, and gorgeous original cover art. We're very, very excited about it. Subscribe now to make sure you get your copy of the issue in the mail ! The cover story? That will be available for subscribers to read digitally next week. And the actual Grand Theft Auto VI game? That releases November 19. That doesn't help you right now . Thankfully, we have weekend recommendations below that you can play right now. But before all that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week. Cover Reveal – Grand Theft Auto VI Check Out The Design Document For Sonic Adventure 2's Iconic City Escape Level One Of Mouthwashing Publisher Critical Reflex's Demos Made Me Gag (Plus, Three Other Games I Can't Wait For) Final Fantasy VII Revelation Preview - Playing Chapter 1 Gave Me Exactly What I Was Looking For After A Disappointing And Overwhelming Gamescom Demo StarCraft Devs Answer Our Biggest Questions at BlizzCon | Interview Control Resonant Review - Fun, Frustration, And Fin Again Control Resonant Marcus Stewart I wrote in my review of this sequel to Control that I love the storytelling, characters, and world, but that the enjoyable combat suffers from way-too-tanky enemies. Thankfully, Remedy swiftly released a day-one patch addressing this very concern . Although I haven’t yet tested the game to see how much it remedies my biggest criticism, I feel even better about recommending Control Resonant. Fans of the first game will have plenty to love and more, as Resonant boasts the same alluring surrealism and fascinating lore as the original, only blown out and spread across a big city. Dylan Faden’s powers make traversing a distorted and visually impressive Manhattan like a superhero feel appropriately cool, and the action only gets deeper and more entertaining as the story progresses. Boasting a strong cast and several memorable moments, Dylan’s adventure is a worthy successor to his sister Jesse’s. Silent Hill: Townfall Kyle Hilliard Silent Hill has been on an impressive streak (as long as you don't think too much about the bizarre 2024 streaming series, Silent Hill: Ascension, or the recent 2026 film, Return to Silent Hill ), and Silent Hill: Townfall does not break the streak. Since deciding to go all back in on the franchise, Konami has been doing a good job of enlisting development partners that all seem to understand what makes the series work. Townfall is not without its shortcomings, which primarily lie in the unfair difficulty of its stealth and combat, but the mood is spot on. I also enjoyed the narrative, which is about corporate nihilism among other fascinating and emotional topics. It also features Terry O'Quinn (of Lost fame) in a prominent role, and he is an actor born to be in a Silent Hill game. You can read Game Informer 's Silent Hill: Townfall review by following the link. EA Sports FC 27 Brian Shea If you're still buzzing from World Cup fever, EA Sports FC 27 is out now. Though this new version doesn't change up a ton from its predecessor, it does give you more control of the players on the pitch, requiring more strategy as you push toward the goal. Off the field, a new social playground called The Grounds funnels players toward the multiplayer features, while continued refinements to Ultimate Team and the Career modes offer more long-form options. You can read Game Informer 's EA Sports FC 27 review by following the link. Kingdom Rush 6: Genesis Matt Miller It's pretty rare that I'll step in to offer a full-throated endorsement for a mobile game, but Kingdom Rush is one of those consistently fun series that always manages to pull me in. The new (sixth!) installment just released this week, and its tower-defense formula remains as fun as ever. While the game will feel mostly familiar to returning fans, Ironhide Game Studio has gone to pains to add some new twists to this iteration, including additional replayability for each of the 18 stages through five unique victory paths for each. The game has a whimsical presentation that belies the high challenge that can define some of the later stages. If you want an approachable game on your mobile device for wherever you're headed this weekend, it's a sure bet. It's also on Steam if that's your preference! Wardogs Eric Van Allen There's been a hunger in the FPS space writ large, I think; a desire for the days of server browsers, lively interactions, and team-based asymmetrical warfare. Wardogs, an Early Access game from Bulkhead currently dominating the Steam charts, ticks all of those boxes. It's easy enough to understand that Battlefield fans can hop in, but it still veers plenty hard into the military sim to have plenty of craftsmanship in your chosen niche. Be a supply driver or builder, constructing forward operating bases, or a helicopter pilot ferrying freshly respawned fighters to the field, or one of those grunts, keeping a body in the hot zone at all times; anything you do builds towards capturing and holding the zone, and accruing your account match-over-match cash in the process. Wardogs has become a nightly ritual for my group, and has been the closest I've felt to days of scrolling Battlefield 1942 servers in ages. Twisted Tower Wesley LeBlanc Twisted Tower does not try to hide its BioShock inspiration. Instead, it embraces it, using what players know of BioShock to set expectations and surprise; after playing through its story in about 8 hours in just two sittings, I can now add "delight." It takes place in the 20th Century and stars a man trying to save his love. To do so, he must travel to the Twisted Tower amusement park, a mix of BioShock's Rapture and Walt Disney World, with the abandoned twistedness you'd expect from the former and the hokey thrills and theming you'd expect from the latter. Using first-person, mostly gun-focused combat and some unlockable toys that give you abilities like dash and grapple, you will traverse five themed levels as you make your way up the titular landmark. All the while, Mr. Twister goads and mocks you along the way, in a very Andrew Ryan-esque way. Of course, there are narrative twists, scares, lots of blood, and plenty of demented employees who haven't clocked out of their Twisted Tower shift yet, awaiting you in each, and it remains fun from start to finish. It can feel a bit rudimentary in how much it leans on its inspirations, but it's one of the best BioShock-likes I've played in a minute, and it's perfect for an exciting weekend gaming jaunt. Shinobi: Art Of Vengeance Brian Shea Shinobi: Art of Vengeance was one of the best action games from last year, but the Switch version wasn't quite as amazing as the other platforms. Sega hopes to remedy that with this week’s Switch 2 edition. Whether you're acrobatically exploring, slicing through hordes of enemies, or taking on daunting boss fights, Shinobi: Art of Vengeance is one that no fan of 2D action games should miss. You can read Game Informer 's Shinobi: Art of Vengeance review by following the link. Tabletop Pick – A-Way Matt Miller This recent card game is packed inside a tiny box that belies a surprisingly rich (if brisk) tactical play experience. You are charting a route for your spaceship to get from point A to B, gradually laying out square cards that will let you cross the far reaches of space. However, certain routes are only one-way, and specific actions (including those played by your opponents) can rotate the cards and block a previously accessible path. As much as you’re aiming to speed to your own finish, you’re looking for ways to block your opponents. That adds a mean streak of play interaction that will delight many, but frustrate others. But the short playthrough length lessens the sting of being messed with, making this an extremely fun filler game in between other larger experiences during your evening of play.
